gether of them in the winter in the

towns and the outskirts of cities, where they

are not the untimely and foolish visitors from

winter visitors are the summer robins of the
far North, for in summer the robin spreads
over the whole northern part of the cont-
inent, almost to the Arctic regions. The rob-
ins that first come to us in the spring have
spent the winter in the Middle states. They
make us but transient visit, and pass on
northward to their own summer homes, while
their place is filled later by our own summer
birds, which may have spent the winter far
south.

In their winter haunts in the South the
robins gather at times in immense flocks,
particularly at their favorite roosting places

No one who is interested in American
politics can fail to be struck by the pe-
culiar taste displayed by the people in
their selection of political terms. Writ

phrases. True, many of these are

language, either as words which pass
into general use, or as expressions to be
looked for in encyclopedias, where they
stand for some episode of past political

political manipulation of which Gerry's
Gerry was the originator, caucus and
bulldoze. Among those which call
to mind particular political episodes are
"Hunker," "Barnburners," "Losofoco"
and "So Liberal." The taste displayed by
the people in the selection of the phrases
destined to live is most extraordinary.
Hundreds of words may be coined, all
of which the people reject most con-
temptuously and absolutely refuse to
adopt. Suddenly, however, another will
appear. It may have no advantage in
sound or sense over the hundred which
failed to find popular approval, but for
some mysterious reason it is caught up,
and almost at once it comes into popu-
lar use.

guage. Often the infant words act in
a most independent manner and take

who are responsible for their birth

United States Consul General at Port au Prince, arrived in this city to-day as passenger on the American steamer Haytien Republic, from Port au Prince. He tells a remarkable story of outrageous treatment, at the hands of the Haytien Government while acting Consul General. Mr. Van Boukelen married a Haytien woman, and, at the end of his term of office, he took up the business of dealing in the paper money of the native Government. In this he made considerable money, and then he desired to invest part of his gains in real estate, but this was forbidden by law of issue, which denies that right to any non-native born citizen.

He evaded the law, however, and purchased a piece of property in Port au Prince, which transaction reaching the ears of President Solomon, the Chief Magistrate of the Republic, he ousted Van Boukelen from office and had him locked up in a dark dungeon in the Government prison at Port au Prince. Here his only companions were negroes of the most bad type, many of them murderers and thieves and robbers, and very often the prison, which is a small and wretched structure, built on low, swampy ground, was crowded with nearly 100 prisoners. Mr. Van Boukelen being the only white man among them.
